newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. cancels envoy's Israel trip on settlements.
newsitem.headline: U.N. cancels envoy's Israel trip on settlements.

text.p: The United Nations said on Monday it was cancelling a planned mission to Israel to discuss the building of settlements in East Jerusalem because of what it called unacceptable conditions imposed by Israel.
"The restrictions imposed on the scope of the mission by the government of Israel were not acceptable to the United Nations," spokesman Fred Eckhard said.
"Regrettably it now appears that the mission will not be taking place since Secretary-General Kofi Annan needs to report to the General Assembly by June 25," he said.

The General Assembly, in an April 25 emergency special session, demanded an immediate halt to the construction of an Israeli settlement in East Jerusalem and called for an end to all assistance to "illegal Israeli activities" in the occupied territories.
The resolution, adopted by a 143-3 vote with ll abstentions, asked Annan to "monitor the situation and to submit a report" within two months."

U.N. sources said Israel wanted no reference to the resolution in the talks with Israeli officials and any discussions the U.N. envoy would have with officials outside the Israeli government, such as Palestinians, could not be included in the report.
Israel's U.N. mission said there had been no need for the General Assembly session and the assembly did not specifically require a special visit.
"Israel felt all along that there was no need for the meeting of the emergency special session to discuss an issue which was discused several times before," charge d'affaires David Peleg said.
"The resolution of the emergency special session requested the secretary-general to monitor the situation but did not request him to send an envoy," he said in response to queries.

"In spite of that, Israel was ready to discuss with the secretary-general proposed parameters which would enable a visit by his representative upon invitation by the government of Israel to visit the area, without harming the peace process," he said, adding: "Regrettably, those proposals were not accepted by the secretary-general."

Annan and the proposed envoy -- Kieran Prendergast, a Briton who is U.N. undersecretary-general for political affairs -- had exchanged letters since the beginning of May in connection with the trip and consulted with Israeli diplomats.
Eckhard said Annan would now make his report "without the benefit of a representative visiting the area."
